prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Some feel rain. Some feel the beetle startle in its ghost-part when the bark slips. Some feel musk. Asleep against each other in the whiskey dark, scarcely there. When it falls apart, some feel the moondark air drop its motes to the patch-thick slopes of snow. Tiny blinkings of ice from the oak, a boot-beat that comes and goes, the line of prayer you can follow from the dusking wind to the snowy owl it carries. Some feel sunlight well up in blood-vessels below the skin and wish there had been less to lose. Knowing how it could have been, pale maples drowsing like a second sleep above our temperaments. Do I imagine there is any place so safe it can’t be snapped? Some feel the rivers shift, blue veins through soil, as if the smokestacks were a long dream of exhalation. The lynx lets its paws skim the ground in snow and showers. The wildflowers scatter in warm tints until the second they are plucked. You can wait to scrape the ankle-burrs, you can wait until Mercury the early star underdraws the night and its blackest districts. And wonder. Why others feel through coal-thick night that deeply colored garnet star. Why sparring and pins are all you have. Why the earth cannot make its way towards you.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Some, Asleep, When

outputs.L1: Some feel rain. Some feel the beetle startle in its ghost-part when the bark slips. Some feel musk. Asleep against one another in the whiskey-dark, scarcely there. When it falls apart, some feel the moon-dark air release its motes onto the patch-thick slopes of snow: tiny blinkings of ice from the oak, a boot-beat that comes and goes, the line of prayer you can follow from the dusking wind to the snowy owl it carries. Some feel sunlight well up in the blood vessels beneath the skin and wish there had been less to lose, knowing how it could have been, pale maples drowsing like a second sleep above our temperaments. Do I imagine there is any place so safe it cannot be snapped? Some feel the rivers shift, blue veins through soil, as though the smokestacks were a long dream of exhalation. The lynx lets its paws skim the ground through snow and showers. The wildflowers scatter in warm tints until the second they are plucked. You can wait to scrape away the ankle-burrs; you can wait until Mercury, the early star, underdraws the night and its blackest districts. And wonder: why others feel, through coal-thick night, that deeply colored garnet star. Why sparring and pins are all you have. Why the earth cannot make its way toward you.
outputs.L2:
Rain reaches certain people. Others sense the beetle’s phantom self recoil as bark peels away, or notice the odor of musk. Bodies sleep pressed together in darkness stained by whiskey, nearly vanished. As things break down, there are those who perceive moonless air releasing specks onto snow-covered, uneven hillsides: minute flashes of ice falling from an oak, the intermittent thud of a boot, and a thread of prayer traceable from the twilight wind to the snowy owl borne upon it.

Some sense sunshine gathering in the vessels beneath their skin and long for there to have been less at stake. They understand what might have happened while pale maples drift above our dispositions in a sleep beyond sleep. I ask myself whether any refuge can be secure enough to resist being broken.

Others detect rivers changing course like blue arteries beneath the earth, as though the smokestacks had merely been an extended dream of breathing out. Through snow and rain, the lynx barely brushes the ground with its feet. Wildflowers spread their warm shades only until the instant someone picks them. There is time to postpone scraping burrs from the ankle; time to wait until Mercury, the morning star, sketches the underside of night and its deepest black regions.

Then comes the wondering: why some people, across a darkness dense as coal, can sense that richly hued, garnet-like star; why struggle and sharp points are the only things left to you; and why the earth is unable to move in your direction.
outputs.L3:
The text evokes a heightened sensitivity to subtle natural phenomena, moving through impressions of rain and musk, ice and wind, flowing rivers, and elusive wildlife. These details create an atmosphere in which even the faintest scent, sound, or movement carries emotional significance. The winter landscape is especially fragile and dreamlike: snow softens the world, moon-dark air obscures familiar forms, pale maples stand like apparitions, and fleeting sounds briefly disturb the stillness before disappearing.

Within this delicate setting, the speaker reflects on loss and imagines how life might have unfolded differently. This backward-looking meditation is accompanied by uncertainty about safety and belonging. The speaker questions whether any place can offer genuine refuge when both the natural world and human experience are marked by change.

Nature is therefore portrayed as beautiful but impermanent. Wildflowers bloom vividly, yet can be plucked almost as soon as they appear; landscapes that seem stable may suddenly fracture or fall away. Such images suggest that beauty is inseparable from vulnerability and that every moment of connection contains the possibility of loss.

The closing questions deepen the text’s sense of isolation and longing. The speaker yearns for a more intimate bond with the earth and for access to sensations or forms of understanding that others seem able to experience more fully. The result is a poignant meditation on transience, solitude, and the human desire to feel rooted in a world that is constantly changing.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a world shaped by vulnerability, loss, and estrangement from nature. Rather than developing these ideas through a clear narrative, it relies on fragmented sensory images—shifts in weather, glimpses of animals, delicate plants, and encroaching darkness. These details create an atmosphere of uncertainty, as though both the speaker and the landscape are exposed to forces they cannot control. Nature appears beautiful and alive, yet it is never fully comforting. Its beauty is temporary, and its living forms seem fragile, threatened, or already disappearing.

This instability gives the poem a strong emotional tension. Images that might ordinarily suggest shelter, renewal, or belonging are shadowed by danger and separation. Changes in light and weather emphasize how quickly safety can vanish, while the presence of vulnerable animals and plants reflects the speaker’s own sense of helplessness. The fragmented structure reinforces this experience: the world cannot be understood as a harmonious whole but is encountered in brief, disconnected impressions. Darkness becomes both a physical presence and a symbol of grief, isolation, and the limits of human understanding.

At the same time, the poem expresses a deep longing for connection. The speaker appears to seek intimacy with the earth, hoping that attention to its smallest details might overcome feelings of alienation. Yet the natural world remains distant, independent, and easily damaged. Human beings may admire it and depend upon it, but they cannot possess or permanently protect it. The poem therefore suggests that beauty and safety are fleeting conditions rather than lasting certainties. Its sadness comes from the recognition that the desire to belong to the earth is powerful, even as the earth remains vulnerable and ultimately beyond human reach.
outputs.L5: Some dreams arrive quietly, like moonlight slipping through a window. When the whole house is asleep, they unfold in the darkness—soft stories of distant places, forgotten faces, and roads not yet taken. By morning, most have vanished, but some remain, waiting to be remembered.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem about disconnection, grief, and the uneven ways people experience nature, using winter imagery, animals, stars, rivers, and industrial landscapes.
counterfactuals.output:
**Winter, Unevenly**

Winter arrives differently for each of us. On the hill, it lays a white hand over the pines and hushes the fox into a flame moving between drifts. Downriver, it hardens in the mouths of pipes, crusts the chain-link fences, settles gray on the roofs of warehouses where the night shift clocks in beneath sodium lamps. Some wake to deer printing the yard with delicate questions. Others wake to the freight train splitting dawn, its iron grief carried for miles.

Since you left, the world has continued without agreement. Starlings gather above the refinery, turning and turning as if one dark thought could become a body. The river takes whatever it is given—snowmelt, oil sheen, the moon broken into trembling coins. I stand on one bank while memory stands on the other, waving with your hands. Between us, black water keeps its terrible appointment with the sea.

At night the stars seem clean, but only from far away. In the city they are erased by the orange breath of factories; in the fields they multiply until loneliness has no ceiling. A child in an apartment names one bright point through the glass. A hunter beneath the frozen constellations listens for the crack of branches. A woman sleeping near the underpass folds cardboard against the wind. The same cold enters each life by a different door.

Even the animals know unevenness. The owl has the whole white meadow for its silence. The rat has the warm machinery beneath the mill. Elk cross the mountain road where headlights briefly make them holy, then vanish into logged dark. Along the canal, geese stand on one leg beside the outflow, mist rising around them like a counterfeit spring.

I used to believe nature was where we went to be healed: the cedar path, the blue hour, the clean snow receiving every footprint. Now I know the earth is not one country. Some inherit orchards; some inherit smokestacks. Some hear rivers singing over stones; some hear them cough beneath concrete. Grief, too, is distributed without mercy. It floods one house, passes another like weather, freezes in the throat of someone who must still rise, dress, and take the bus past the shining silos.

Still, this morning, a coyote walks the rail line. Thin as hunger, careful as prayer, it places its paws between the ties and follows the tracks beyond the factories. Above it, the last star burns through exhaust. Below it, under ice and rust, the river keeps moving—dark, divided, carrying everything away, carrying everything together.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental poem beginning with the repeated phrase “Some feel,” contrasting people who feel deeply connected to the earth with a speaker who feels emotionally stranded.
counterfactuals.output:
Some feel, some feel  
the earth breathing beneath the pavement—  
a dark lung  
lifting roots, stones, sleeping seeds.

Some feel rain enter them  
as if the body were a field  
and every drop  
remembered where to go.

Some feel the small republic of moss,  
the parliament of crows,  
the moon tugging the hidden water  
through their wrists.

They kneel.  
They listen.  
The soil says *home*  
in a language older than doors.

I press my ear down too.

Nothing—

only the far machinery  
of my own blood,  
only a coastline without a sea,  
a compass worrying  
its one broken direction.

Some feel held  
by the planet’s green hand.

I feel the hand withdraw.

Between me and the world:  
a long salt room,  
an unplugged horizon,  
a boat made entirely  
of leaving.

Some feel, some feel—

and I, stranded inland,  
keep sending up flares  
to the roots.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a single-paragraph, surreal nature poem in a contemporary literary style. Include rain, a beetle, whiskey-dark sleep, snow falling from an oak, a snowy owl, maples, smokestacks, a lynx, wildflowers, Mercury, and a garnet-colored star.
counterfactuals.output: Rain stitches the meadow to its reflection while a beetle, green as a secret, shoulders the moon through the grass; beneath the hill, we enter whiskey-dark sleep and dream of snow falling from an oak in midsummer, each white leaf opening an eye. A snowy owl crosses the maples without disturbing their red arithmetic, and beyond them the smokestacks exhale long blue animals into the dusk. Somewhere a lynx moves through wildflowers, its paws gathering silence, while Mercury trembles backward along the horizon and a garnet-colored star lowers itself into the river, hissing softly, as if the night had touched a wound to water.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a melancholic ecopoem that blends intimate loss with environmental imagery. Use unusual compound words, dreamlike syntax, vivid sensory details, and end with a series of anguished questions about why the earth remains unreachable.
counterfactuals.output:
After you left, the house grew lichenward—  
cups furred green in the sink,  
your pillow breathing its small salt weather.  
At night I heard the refrigerator  
dreaming of glaciers, blue and unbroken,  
while somewhere the real ice  
unstitched its ancient sleeves into the sea.

I carried your name like rainmetal  
under my tongue. Even the garden knew:  
tomatoes split their red mouths,  
bees staggered home through pesticide dusk,  
and the pear tree, fever-leaved,  
dropped its hard little planets  
before they could sweeten.

Once, your hand in mine  
was a warm animal crossing.  
Now rivers pass through my sleep  
with oil-rainbows for eyes;  
herons lift from the shallows  
like torn gray letters,  
addressed to no surviving country.

In the forest’s ash-throat  
I thought I heard you calling—  
or wind worrying the blackened pines,  
or roots belowground whispering  
in their mycelium-dark, their ruinbright grammar.  
I knelt. The soil smelled of iron,  
wet bark, and something almost human:  
the last heat leaving a body.

Still, mornings arrive honey-colored,  
cruel with birdsong.  
Still, the ocean combs its plastic hair.  
Still, I set two plates at the table  
while droughtlight gathers in the windows  
and moths, those dust-winged widows,  
bruise themselves against the moon.

Where have you gone, beneath what smokebloom sky?  
Why does the ground recoil from my listening?  
Why do the roots close their doors when I call?  
Why can I taste the rain but never enter it?  
Why does every road end at a fence of flame?  
Why does the earth keep turning its wounded face away?  
Why is it beneath me, around me, inside me—  
and still, still unreachable?
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a dense, image-rich prose poem about longing for safety in a fragile world, moving through darkness into fleeting light and back again. Avoid rhyme and conventional narrative; favor associative transitions, personification, and haunting rhetorical questions.
counterfactuals.output:
At night the house forgets its own walls. Plaster loosens into weather; every window becomes a black mouth tasting the wind. I lie beneath a thin quilt printed with vanished flowers and listen to the pipes rehearse their small catastrophes. Somewhere, a siren combs the streets with a red tooth. Somewhere, glass waits inside the stone. What can the body trust when even sleep keeps one eye open?

I want safety the way a seed wants the locked dark—not as escape, but as a room where breaking might mean beginning. Yet the earth shivers around its buried engines. The roots clutch one another. Bridges dream of falling and wake trembling in their bolts. Even the moon seems borrowed, a pale plate carried over rooftops by an invisible, unsteady hand.

Then morning enters through a crack no wider than a breath.

Dust rises, astonished into gold. A cup on the table gathers warmth along its rim. The curtains lift their frail wrists. For one moment, the world is held together by steam, by the blue vein in someone’s eyelid, by a sparrow landing on a bent antenna as if ruin were merely another branch. Who has not mistaken this tenderness for a promise? Who has not stood inside a blade of sunlight and called it shelter?

Outside, puddles keep pieces of sky without asking whether the sky will remain. A child’s red mitten lies beside the gutter, still shaped around an absent hand. The trees, stripped nearly bare, hoard a few leaves like letters they cannot bear to burn. I pass beneath them carrying my heart as one carries a glass of water through a crowd: both hands, no sudden movement.

But light is a guest with its coat already buttoned.

By afternoon, clouds close over the roofs. Shadows return to their assigned corners and begin enlarging them. The stairwell fills with the smell of rain and old iron. Doors settle deeper into their frames. In the distance, thunder drags a cabinet across the heavens. Is there any sanctuary that does not hear the storm practicing its name? Any embrace without the faint architecture of departure?

Night comes back wearing the faces of all we could not save. The house counts us by our breathing. The floorboards whisper beneath their varnish. Still, I place a lamp beside the window—not to defeat the dark, only to give it one small, breakable star.

How else shall we live, if not around this trembling flame?

How else, knowing the glass is thin, the wind awake, the match already shortening in the hand?
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
